sources.bodyExcerpt: Guitar Pedal X - GPX Blog - Fortin's latest Kali Pre-Amp Distortion Pedal captures those classic 80's California Modded Marshall Sounds of Jose Arredondo ao link News GPX AI Forums Notifications Popular Highlights 4 of a Kind 12 Degrees of Saturation ArtistArray Best in Class Best of Brands Builder Profiles Colours Expo Guitar Pedal 101 Iconic Gear In Memoriam Pedal Chain Pedal Planet Trifecta Versus Index News GPX AI Forums Notifications Popular Highlights 4 of a Kind 12 Degrees of Saturation ArtistArray Best in Class Best of Brands Builder Profiles Colours Expo Guitar Pedal 101 Iconic Gear In Memoriam Pedal Chain Pedal Planet Trifecta Versus Index Enter a search term Search Remember Login Register | Reset Password Xploration • Curation • Recommendation News GPX AI Forums Notifications Popular Highlights 4 of a Kind 12 Degrees of Saturation ArtistArray Best in Class Best of Brands Builder Profiles Colours Expo Guitar Pedal 101 Iconic Gear In Memoriam Pedal Chain Pedal Planet Trifecta Versus Index News GPX AI Forums Notifications Popular Highlights 4 of a Kind 12 Degrees of Saturation ArtistArray Best in Class Best of Brands Builder Profiles Colours Expo Guitar Pedal 101 Iconic Gear In Memoriam Pedal Chain Pedal Planet Trifecta Versus Index Enter a search term Search Remember Login Register | Reset Password Filter content by area of interest Amps Boost and Overdrive Delay Distortion Fuzz Guitars Modulation Pitch Reverb Utility All All Fortin's latest Kali Pre-Amp Distortion Pedal captures those classic 80's California Modded Marshall Sounds of Jose Arredondo Aug 5, 2025 08:00 by Stefan Karlsson Distortion Dual-Drive Fortin Amps Marshall Style Distortion PreAmp + - Full Article Read Summary Key Points Fortin’s Kali is a Pre-Amp Pedal derived from the 2019 Cali amp, capturing Jose Arredondo’s modifications to Plexi and JCM800 Marshall Amps. It completes Fortin’s High Gain Pedal Trifecta with the Natas and Meshuggah. It features Bass, Mid, Treble, Master, Vintage/Raw/Saturated, Gain 2 and Gain 1 three-way switches, plus Channel 1/2 and On/Bypass footswitches. Ola Englund is noted as a fan. The Kali will be compared with the Sinvertek MGAT-1 Golden Era and Tsakalis AudioWorks Room #40. It is available from the Fortin Webstore for $299, with European distribution expected later. Jose Arredondo definitely seems to be flavour of the month these days - with Friedman having just recently released its ’Tribute’ Amp Head - based on that Amp Technician’s legendary 80’s Marshall Mods. Where Fortin’s equivalent Cali amp was launched all the way back in 2019. This renamed Kali is the Pre-Amp Pedal derivation of that specific amp - making use of all those killer Jose Arredondo Modifications to Plexi and JCM800 Marshall Amps in particular. Fortin very much seems to be on a roll these days - with this Kali completing its High Gain Pedal Trifecta - alongside its superb Natas and Meshuggah forebears. Since I own those two already - it’s kind of a no-brainer that I should go for this one too - to complete the set! I love a good Marshall Preamp - will be interesting to see how it stacks up against the Sinvertek MGAT-1 Golden Era and Tsakalis AudioWorks Room #40 - this cover similar territory! Ola Englund seems to love the Kali - and he’s usually on the ball for these sorts of things - so the Kali really promises well. There’s also the recent Fourteen Modded Tube Screamer Fortin pedal to consider - which I have indeed thought about, but not assigned a priority yet. The Kali would certainly be prioritised over the Fourteen. Controls - Bass, Mid, Treble, Master - Vintage / Raw / Saturated, Gain 2 - 1 / 0 / 2 (Bright), Gain 1 - 1 / 0 / 2 (Bright), Channel 1/2 Footswitch, On/Bypass Footswitch. This is a smart 2-Channel Pre-Amp - with the mods presumably rendered courtesy of those 3 x 3-way switches. With a pedigree of modifying and designing amps (within the realms of Marshall, Vox, Hi-Watt, Randall and Fortin Amplification) that spans well over 30 years, Mike is widely accepted as the harbinger of complex modern high-Gain tones. The Killer Kali module is based on the Fortin Cali amp (complete with the Violence and Sat boosts) that brought the legendary Cali and KK++ mods to a production model; this British voiced monster will allow Synergy users to fully experience this extraordinary piece of modern sonic art. In stock Fortin Killer Kali Preamp Module quantity Add to cart Description Technical Media Downloads The Killer Kali is a two channel pre-amp, designed to work exclusively in the Synergy Amp systems. Each channel is completely independent and enjoys its own tone stack and multiple tone shaping features. Gain 1 and Gain 2 Cascaded Gain stages. Gain 1 controls the first gain stage whereas Gain 2 controls the second gain stage. Bright Switches 3-way Bright switch for each Gain control. At the top is the Brightest, most aggressive tone. The Bright switches are directly connected to the Gain control so the higher you have the Gain, the less the Bright tends to affect the tone (similar to the Bright control on a standard Plexi Amp). In the middle it is full range, so is unaffected by the Gain control. At the bottom position, the Brightness is similar to the classic Bright control on an 800 2203. Violence Switch In the down position, it utilizes the three Gain stages, when up it brings in an additional tube Gain stage. Sat (saturation) Switch Down, no change. Up, adds another clipping circuit that increases compression and Gain. EQ Shape A three-way switch that changes the points of the EQ. Up is a typical M style tone stack, the middle is more F style (more scooped) and then all the way down is “somewhere in between” - shifting up the treble and midrange. sources.bodyExcerpt: Fortin Natas Distortion | Delicious Audio Creative Pedals Creative Delay Tape Delay W/ Reverb Delay Distortion Fuzz Overdrive Dual Gain Dirt Boost Compr. + Dynamics Dynamics EQ Filter Wah Filter+EQ Lo-Fi 8 Bit Lo-fi Chorus Flanger Phaser Tremolo Uni-Vibe Modulation Pitch Shifter Octaver pitch Multiverb Reverb Spring Reverb Reverb CV In Granular Synth Pedals Synth Effect Guides Monthly Lists Shopping Guides Coverage Schedule Facebook Stompbox Exhibit Fortin Natas Distortion Updated Oct. 25, 2023 | by Paolo De Gregorio The Fortin Natas Distortion is a pedal version of one the company’s now disontinued, but very popular in the mid aughts, Natas guitar amp. Forting describes itself as “the heaviest company in the guitar world,” and for good reason: their line of amps and pedals is geared towards heavy guitarists, and the Natas is no exception. The controls of the Natas pedal closely match the ones of the amp, with two gain stages (Volume and Gain), a regular 3-band EQ, and two small knobs any metal guitarist would want to see in a distortion pedal, called Grind and Girth . While the regular EQ is applied after the distortion, these two are filters affecting high and low frequencies of the signal before it hits the distortion stage, widening the palette of tones, from sharper to darker and full bodied. The Mid Shift switch toggle lets you pick two different frequencies to boost or cut via the Mid knob, allowing, amont other things, for scooped and lo-mids-heavy tones. sources.bodyExcerpt: Sinister by Foxgear | RockBoard | PedalPedia Skip to main content LOG IN EXPLORE Foxgear Sinister LOG IN TO SUGGEST IMPROVEMENTS DISTORTION Description The Sinister is one potent piece of metal distortion gear. Thanks to Foxgear’s pioneering distortion circuit “DynaFET™” made of multi-stage Class A FET, the Sinister is capable of reaching an insane amount of gain. sources.bodyExcerpt: Quick Hit: Foxpedal Defector Fuzz Review — Precision, Clarity, and Dynamic Range in a Compact Analog Circuit | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / practice tips practice tips Quick Hit: Foxpedal Defector Fuzz Review — Precision, Clarity, and Dynamic Range in a Compact Analog Circuit By Liam Carter July 10, 2026 The Foxpedal Defector Fuzz is not another vintage-inspired clone—it’s a precision-engineered, modern analog fuzz pedal designed for dynamic responsiveness, harmonic fidelity, and studio-grade consistency. Measuring 118 mm × 68 mm × 52 mm (4.65″ × 2.68″ × 2.05″) with true-bypass switching and a discrete silicon transistor circuit (2N5088 and 2N5089 matched pair), it delivers 32 dB of gain with Design Philosophy and Circuit Architecture Foxpedal, based in Portland, Oregon, positions the Defector as a ‘fidelity-first’ fuzz. Its core departure from classic designs lies in intentional rejection of passive tone-sucking networks and unregulated bias drift. While most silicon fuzzes (e.g., Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi v1) use cascaded gain stages with RC filtering that attenuates low-end and compresses dynamics, the Defector employs a dual-stage active EQ buffer pre- and post-fuzz core. This architecture isolates the fuzz circuit from pickup impedance variations—a critical factor often overlooked in practice scenarios where players switch between Stratocasters (7.2 kΩ DC resistance) and Les Pauls (14.8 kΩ). Transistor Matching and Thermal Stability Each Defector unit ships with hand-matched 2N5088 (Q1, input stage) and 2N5089 (Q2, output stage) transistors, selected for h FE within ±3% tolerance (measured at V CE = 1V, I C = 1mA). This tight matching reduces inter-stage imbalance and ensures consistent clipping symmetry. Crucially, Foxpedal mounts both transistors on thermally coupled copper pads, achieving No Passive Tone Stack, No Compromise Many pedals insert passive tone controls (e.g., the treble bleed network in the Dunlop Fuzz Face) that load the circuit and degrade high-frequency transient response. The Defector omits such networks entirely. Instead, its single-knob ‘Tone’ control adjusts a fully active Baxandall-style EQ centered at 1.8 kHz, with ±12 dB boost/cut range and Q = 1.4. This preserves signal integrity while offering surgical shaping—essential when practicing legato phrasing or harmonic minor sequences where upper-mid clarity determines intelligibility. Key Controls and Operational Behavior The Defector features three knobs: Volume (output level, calibrated to unity at 12 o’clock), Fuzz (gain staging, logarithmic taper), and Tone (active EQ). All pots are Alpha 9mm sealed units rated for 200,000 cycles. Unlike pedals with ambiguous gain labeling (e.g., “Sustain” on the Electro-Harmonix Big Muff), the Fuzz control delivers linear, repeatable gain increase: from 18 dB at 9 o’clock to 32 dB at 3 o’clock, verified via oscilloscope measurement using a 1 kHz sine wave at −20 dBu input. Volume Control Precision The Volume knob operates with 0.5 dB resolution per 15° rotation near unity—meaning subtle adjustments (e.g., dropping volume by 1.5 dB for cleaner chord comping) are physically precise and audibly distinct. This granularity matters during metronome-based practice: reducing output by exactly 2 dB while maintaining identical pick attack allows focused study of dynamic shading without altering tonal character. Fuzz Knob Linearity and Sweet Spots At 10–2 o’clock, the Fuzz control yields a ‘transparent overdrive’ zone ideal for blues phrasing—retaining string texture and harmonic nuance. Between 2–4 o’clock, it transitions into singing sustain with even-order harmonic emphasis (measured 2nd harmonic at −14.2 dB relative to fundamental). From 4–6 o’clock, odd-order harmonics dominate (3rd at −12.8 dB), delivering articulate distortion suited for jazz-rock fusion lines. sources.bodyExcerpt: Guitar Pedal X - GPX Blog - Foxpedal's Vixen Dimensional Drive is even more appealing in the flesh and has a Wonderful Depth of Harmonics ao link News GPX AI Forums Notifications Popular Highlights 4 of a Kind 12 Degrees of Saturation ArtistArray Best in Class Best of Brands Builder Profiles Colours Expo Guitar Pedal 101 Iconic Gear In Memoriam Pedal Chain Pedal Planet Trifecta Versus Index News GPX AI Forums Notifications Popular Highlights 4 of a Kind 12 Degrees of Saturation ArtistArray Best in Class Best of Brands Builder Profiles Colours Expo Guitar Pedal 101 Iconic Gear In Memoriam Pedal Chain Pedal Planet Trifecta Versus Index Enter a search term Search Remember Login Register | Reset Password Xploration • Curation • Recommendation News GPX AI Forums Notifications Popular Highlights 4 of a Kind 12 Degrees of Saturation ArtistArray Best in Class Best of Brands Builder Profiles Colours Expo Guitar Pedal 101 Iconic Gear In Memoriam Pedal Chain Pedal Planet Trifecta Versus Index News GPX AI Forums Notifications Popular Highlights 4 of a Kind 12 Degrees of Saturation ArtistArray Best in Class Best of Brands Builder Profiles Colours Expo Guitar Pedal 101 Iconic Gear In Memoriam Pedal Chain Pedal Planet Trifecta Versus Index Enter a search term Search Remember Login Register | Reset Password Filter content by area of interest Amps Boost and Overdrive Delay Distortion Fuzz Guitars Modulation Pitch Reverb Utility All All Foxpedal's Vixen Dimensional Drive is even more appealing in the flesh and has a Wonderful Depth of Harmonics May 25, 2021 19:00 by Stefan Karlsson Boost Boost and Overdrive Foxpedal Harmonic Overdrive Overdrive + - Full Article Read Summary Key Points Foxpedal’s Vixen Dimensional Drive: striking royal-blue/purple finish and two clipping options — Nanalog N3 Quantum Diode and 1N4148. N3 mode: dense, deep harmonic character with reduced top-end; 1N4148: more open, lighter, less low-end and more high frequency. Medium-gain pedal; typical settings: Gain 12–3 o’clock, Presence ~2:30, Volume ~2 o’clock, Bass and Treble often maxed. Not quite as harmonically rich as a Keeley‑Modded Blues Driver, but close and distinct. John and Bruce Snyder took over Foxpedal on Jan 1, 2018; Quiver Tremolo and Novaplex Delay are nearing completion. As of May, the price was £199, sold via the Foxpedal Webstore. May has been a busy month with quite a number of overdrive pedals new on the scene, and within that company the Vixen Dimensional Drive is a particularly special candidate. It has one of the prettiest enclosures you might ever happen upon - with a really special paint-job of a vibrant shade of Royal Blues which is right on the cusp of Purple - so that in certain lights the pedal appears sort of purple - but is most of the time a really deep and vibrant royal blue. I noted before that one of its clipping options is pretty rare - the Nanalog N3 Quantum Diode. And that’s where most of the fun is to be had - with a particularly appealing dense and deep harmonic character with a little less top-end too. It’s not quite as harmonically rich as my Keeley-Modded Blues Driver - but replaces that pedal for this month at least with something pretty close to that sort of richness - while being distinct to itself. The other 1N4148 Diode flavour is a somewhat more open-pored and slightly lighter touch - with less low-end and more high frequency content. John Snyder of Creation Music and Foxpedal fame explained to me why he did not feel it worthwhile to have a second footswitch to toggle those two modes as they are quite distinct. While I largely deploy the same settings on both - and with Bass and Treble Maxed out. This is very much a medium-gain pedal - where I operate the Gain mostly between 12-3 o’c, Presence at around 2:30 o’c, and Volume adjusted to setup - which on mine is around 2 o’c. There’s plenty of range on-tap here in any case on each control. This is a really versatile and dynamic - and richly harmonic overdrive -

Close Submit Close Quantity + - Add to Cart Features Reviews Q & A Tech Info CC Hybrid2 is based on the classic Fuzz Face circuit, originally available in two versions using germanium or silicon transistors. CC Hybrid2 uses one of each, combining the warm, dark organic tone of germanium with the clarity and sustain of silicon. The Si/Ge transistor pair is selected by ear and biased to deliver a tone with all the best qualities of Germanium and Silicon. CC Hybrid2 is a very stable fuzz that rejects radio transmissions, and the tone does not change with temperature (two common Fuzz Face problems) Hybrid History The original CC Hybrid is named after the Foxrox Captain Coconut (CC) pedal. CC combined a Fuzz Face, Uni-Vibe, and Octavia into one pedal, and it was the first to utilize a Fuzz Face circuit with one silicon and one germanium transistor. Its successor, Captain Coconut2 , was later produced with a plug-in hybrid FuzzCard, in addition to optional all-silicon and all-germanium FuzzCards. The Si/Ge hybrid circuit lived on through the CC Hybrid pedal, produced from 2012-2016. In 2017, it was discontinued and replaced with CC Hybrid2. CONTROLS FUZZ : Typical setting: All the way up, or backed off a little. You can dial in a massive range of great sounds just by playing around with the GRIT control, the FUZZ control, and your guitar’s volume and tone controls. A 1K reverse-log taper pot is used for spreading the range out evenly. GRIT : Typical setting: 12:00. Grit allows you to fine-tune the bias of the transistors. Recreate the sound of miss-matched transistors or a dying battery. Tones range from smooth to gated when fully clockwise. VOLUME : Typical setting: Adjust to match guitar volume or set to maximum for overdriving amp. Increasing the volume also increases the brightness of the Fuzz. POWER : On/off switch for saving battery life when the pedal is not in use. This is a convenience feature for those who use a pedal board and prefer to use a battery. There is no need to unplug the input jack when not in use. The Power On/Off switch shuts off external power as well. Power is automatically disconnected when there is nothing plugged into the input jack. INPUT PAD: This switch adds some resistance at the input of the fuzz. One foot switch $135.15 $67.58 Quantity : Add to cart SKU: RGS-FR-FESTIVAL Category: Other Description Specifications Reviews Details The Festival Overdrive is a dual-mode overdrive. It features a master volume control and a boost channel with both gain and volume controls. There is a selectable clipping/compression circuit and two tone shaping controls – body and bright. One foot switch bypasses the effect and another foot switch selects between the green and red channels (low gain and high gain). Watch Pete Thorn’s demo above to hear the Festival in action. Body control The Body control on Festival is identical to Voice #1 on the Foxrox ZIM pedal. To help explain this control, heres Dave Foxs post at THE GEAR PAGE: Ive been using A Foxrox ZIM pedal on my board for 12 years. I love the voicing knob for getting cool sounds, and I found that while voices 2 through 8 are great for special effects, Voice 1 works more like a tool. It doesn’t really change your tone, it just makes it fit in with the rest of the band when the volume is loud. It’s a knob I adjust for different rooms, different amps, and sometimes I adjust it as the night goes on and the band gets louder. Turn it one way to make it less boomy and more bright, turn it the other way when it sounds thin. Clipping stages Festival gives you two clipping options. The first is a single clipping stage, which is always active. The second is an additional stage which is selected by the Clipping stages switch. This adds a layer of soft clipping at high gain settings. The result is a slightly compressed tone, both in dynamic range and frequency range. Playing harder doesn’t make you louder, it just gets more saturated. Some top and bottom goes away and is replaced with a slight amount of harmonic fizz on the top end. This makes for a more cutting tone when you need your leads to stick out. Main Controls Bypass Foot switch: True bypass with a yellow LED. Boost Foot switch: Switch with dual-color LED to select between gain modes: standard mode (Green) and volume/drive Boost (Red). Master volume: Controls the overall volume of the pedal. Turning it up or down affects both channels equally. This makes it easy to maintain the same rhythm-to-lead volume ratio when you need to turn your overall level up or down. Typical setting is bewteen 9:00 and 1:00. A Linear taper volume pot is used so that rotation of the knob covers a wide usable range. Green drive: This is the rhythm drive setting. Typical setting is around 12:00. Red drive: This controls the high gain channel and there is more available gain on this control compared to the Green Drive control. sources.bodyExcerpt: ZIM Dual Drive by Foxrox Electronics | RockBoard | PedalPedia Skip to main content LOG IN EXPLORE Foxrox Electronics ZIM Dual Drive LOG IN TO SUGGEST IMPROVEMENTS Description ZIM's Channel B voicing section uses 8 cascading stages of phase shift which can be mixed both in and out of phase. This creates an almost limitless palate of tones simulating different amps and mic'ing techniques. ZIM's two channels use plug-in cards, called ZIMcards, for their processing. ZIM comes with a pair of ZIMcards already installed. The current default ZIMcards are Vintage Tube in Channel A and Hot 9 in Channel B. This pair gives a wide range of overdrive sounds. If you'd like us to customize your ZIM pedal with specific ZIMcards, choose Channel A and B cards from the dropdown menu above. Did you ever wish you had a Fuzz with a level boost? Or an Octave with overdrive? Or an overdrive with a switchable treble boost? Distortion and OD in one pedal? With ZIM you can pair up different effects to create your desert island pedal. If your tastes change and you need, for example, Fuzz instead of Distortion, you don't have to change pedals. Swap out the ZIMcard and now your ZIM is a Fuzz pedal. sources.bodyExcerpt: Classics Explore classic Foxrox Electronics pedals from the past, which are no longer in production. These include Captain Coconut, Captain Coconut2, Paradox TZF, Festival, ZIM and others that were retired to make way for new pedals. Skip to Main Content Home History Videos Dealers Classics Contact Hello, Guest | My Account (0) Items 0 Items Toggle navigation Pedals Accessories Specials Home Classics Classics Explore classic Foxrox pedals from the past. Click the images below to view the product's original features. You can also download the owner's manual on each page. ProVibe Last Manufactured in 1994 The first pedal made after registering the Foxrox Electronics name. Accurately produced the sounds of the classic Uni-Vibe effect. Its watery phasing and warm vibrato made it instantly recognizable, and Foxrox made them available in floor and rack-mount units. Captain Coconut Last Manufactured in July, 2001 Octave, Vibe and Fuzz effects in one unit. Captain Coconut brought together three of the most sought-after effects in one easy to use, reliable and great sounding box. All faithful reproductions of vintage effect circuitry, fine-tuned for the best sounds and added flexibility. Captain Coconut2 Last Manufactured in October, 2006 A re-design of the original Captain Coconut effect. CC2 set a new standard in limited production, hand-built guitar effects. The product features included a plug-in fuzz card, envelope controlled speed for the ProVibe, and improved speed control. Paradox TZ F Last Manufactured in October, 2006 An original design...not a clone. Paradox TZF is the first and only flanger of its kind. Through-zero-flanging was done in the '60s using a pair of analog tape decks. TZF recreates that over-the-top flanging sound in a stomp box. Octron Last Manufactured in December, 2016 Octron is an analog octave pedal. It's an organic effect that responds to your playing style/technique, and it takes on a new life when put through other effects. Octave up, down, clean with a little of each mixed...dial in just a hint of octave or make Octron your octave monster! CC Hybrid Fuzz Last Manufactured in September, 2017 CC Hybrid is one of the first pedals to use one germanium and one silicon transistor in the classic Fuzz Face circuit. Hot Silicon Fuzz Last Manufactured in June, 2019 Hot Silicon Fuzz is our take on the original high gain silicon FuzzFace, providing an array of fuzz tones to please even the pickiest players. Festival Overdrive Last Manufactured in December, 2020 The Festival Overdrive is a dual-mode overdrive. It features a master volume control and a boost channel with both gain and volume controls. Octron2 Last Manufactured in May, 2021 Octron2 is a special version of the Foxrox Octron pedal with the addition of individual foot switches with LED for Octave up, Direct, and Octave down. Inspired by feedback from Mahogany Rush guitarist, Frank Marino, improvements were made to the original Octron to arrive at something cool, new and unique. ZIM Dual Drive Last Manufactured in July, 2022 ZIM is a two-channel pedal that you can configure with any combination of Drive, Distortion, Fuzz, Boost and Octave using plug-in ZIMcards. Original Paradox TZF2 Last Manufactured in June, 2018 Paradox TZF2 is an analog Through-Zero Flanger geared towards live performance. Hot Silicon2 Fuzz Last Manufactured in May, 2024 Hot Silicon2 takes us back to 1986 when a young Dave Fox, while working for Dallas Music Industries, Inc, brought the Dallas Arbiter Fuzz Face back from extinction. 2Boost Two-Level Tunable Boost Last Manufactured in May, 2024 2Boost gives you two levels of adjustable clean boost, plus a phase shift filter that works as a powerful tone modifier. Octron4 Last Manufactured in August, 2025 Analog Octave Up, Down, and Direct, each with its own foot switch. Octave Down includes sub-octave sounds. The company is known for its unique and high-quality analog effects pedals, built with love and care in the USA. sources.bodyExcerpt: Frantone Electronics — Grokipedia Search ⌘K Suggest Edit Sign in Sign in History Founding and Early Development (1994–1999) Growth and Operational Milestones (2000s) Challenges, Hiatus, and Relaunch (2010s–Present) Products Core Effects Pedals Custom and Limited Editions Fran Blanche Background and Self-Taught Expertise Leadership and Innovations at Frantone Design Philosophy and Technical Aspects Analog Circuit Design Principles Manufacturing Processes and Quality Control Reception and Legacy Acclaim Among Musicians and Enthusiasts Criticisms, Market Challenges, and Broader Impact References Fact-checked by Grok 8 months ago Frantone Electronics Ara Eve Leo Sal 1x Frantone Electronics is a United States-based boutique manufacturer of hand-crafted analog guitar effects pedals, founded in 1994 by engineer and designer Fran Blanche. [1] The company specializes in original, high-quality designs such as the Peachfuzz fuzz pedal, Vibutron tremolo, and Brooklyn Overdrive, emphasizing limited-production runs built entirely by hand with a focus on tonal excellence. [2] Pioneering the boutique effects movement in the mid-1990s alongside contemporaries like Zachary Vex, Frantone gained a cult following among musicians for its innovative circuits and durable construction, though its small-scale output has kept it somewhat under the radar compared to mass-produced alternatives. [3] Blanche, who handles design, assembly, and repairs personally, has shared insights into the company's processes via her YouTube channel and interviews, highlighting a commitment to analog purity over digital emulation. [4] While praised in niche publications like Tone Report Magazine for superior sound—such as the Vibutron being dubbed "the best analog trem on the market"—Frantone's pedals remain sought-after collector's items due to intermittent production and Blanche's evolving pursuits in electronics and music. [5] History Founding and Early Development (1994–1999) Frantone Electronics was established in 1994 by Fran Blanche, a self-taught electronics engineer, in Lancaster, Pennsylvania , marking it as one of the earliest boutique guitar effects pedal companies. Blanche initially constructed a personal fuzz pedal called the " Fuzzy-Wuzzy " to address her needs in a band setting, driven by dissatisfaction with available commercial options. This prototype laid the groundwork for commercial production, with the company launching formally amid the nascent boutique pedal movement. [3] [6] The inaugural commercial product, the Hep Cat overdrive pedal, entered production by late 1995 after approximately one year of development, reflecting Blanche's emphasis on original analog circuit designs rather than clones of mass-market effects. Early operations involved handmade assembly and faced significant financial challenges, including debt accumulation due to limited initial sales and the realities of entering the music industry without prior business experience. By 1996, the Hep Cat gained traction among musicians seeking high-quality, custom alternatives to mainstream pedals. [3] [6] From 1996 to 1999, Frantone expanded its lineup with innovative designs such as the Peachfuzz fuzz pedal, whose first production run occurred in 1997 and featured novel transistor biasing techniques avoiding traditional diodes for distortion. Other early offerings included the Cream Puff and The Sweet, a germanium fuzz derived from rejected ideas for an Electro-Harmonix Big Muff reissue, showcasing Blanche's focus on custom optocouplers and audio compressors for superior tone control. The company operated on a small scale, prioritizing handcrafted quality over mass production, which positioned it alongside contemporaries like Zachary Vex in fostering the boutique ethos of the late 1990s. Now you can get that same tonal versatility, sensitivity and harmonically rich overdrive in a pedal. The Dirty Shirley Overdrive packs the same intuitive control set as the amplifier, allowing you to dial in your perfect shade of rock in no time. It doesn't matter if you want a high-output cleaner tone for pushing your amp hard or a thick gritty drive that will sit well in any classic to modern rock band, a sweep of the gain control easily gets you there. If you ever want reign in the low end, for a punchier feel, simply flip the side-mounted Tight switch and away you go. If you want to experience the amp’s accolade-garnering tone in the convenience of a pedal, put the Dirty Shirley Overdrive on your board today. British rock at its best Though the Dirty Shirley overdrive can scream with an unabashedly rock ‘n’ roll voice, you’ll be surprised at how truly versatile it is. To get more out of the amp you already have, roll the pedal’s gain knob back, crank the volume and get a killer dirty boost. And of course, roll up the gain and witness how well the pedal responds to every touch and manipulation of your guitar’s controls. Friedman Dirty Shirley amp tone in a compact pedal format Responds to guitar controls and picking nuance exactly like the amp Gain control takes you from gritty to hard rock in no time Ready for your rig The Dirty Shirley Overdrive pedal delivers tube like tone in a small pedal format which can be used either into a clean amp or to boost an already over-driven amp. If your amp, or other overdrive gets a bit loose in the low end, throw ON the Dirty Shirley’s Tight switch to bring back the percussive attack you crave. Authentic tube amplifier sound in a compact pedal Shape your tone with volume, gain, tight switch (side mounted), bass, treble and presence. sources.h1: Friedman Amplification Unveils the Fuzz Fiend and Motor City Drive: Dual-Pedal Breakthroughs in High-Gain Tone Sculpting
sources.description: Friedman Amplification has launched two new boutique overdrive/distortion pedals: the Fuzz Fiend (a dual-stage silicon/germanium fuzz with bias control) and the Motor City Drive (a three-knob, all-analog mid-focused overdrive inspired by Detroit rock tone). Both feature true bypass, 9V DC operation, compact enclosures (3.875" × 2.25" × 1.25" for each), and hand-wired PCBs with premium components including Vishay MCB metal-film resistors, Wima polypropylene coupling caps, and custom-wound CTS 25k audio taper pots.

sources.bodyExcerpt: Friedman Amplification Unveils the Fuzz Fiend and Motor City Drive: Dual-Pedal Breakthroughs in High-Gain Tone Sculpting | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Friedman Amplification Unveils the Fuzz Fiend and Motor City Drive: Dual-Pedal Breakthroughs in High-Gain Tone Sculpting By Liam Carter July 14, 2026 Friedman Amplification has officially entered the high-performance stompbox arena with the simultaneous launch of two meticulously engineered analog pedals: the Fuzz Fiend and the Motor City Drive. Unlike typical product rollouts, these units aren’t rehashes or simplified versions of existing amp circuits — they represent a deliberate expansion of Friedman’s tonal philosophy into the pedal domain, grounded in decades of amplifier design experience and real-world artist collaboration. The Fuzz Fiend delivers a dynamically responsive, touch-sensitive fuzz with selectable silicon or germanium transistor stages and continuous bias modulation, while the Motor City Drive channels the aggressive yet articulate midrange punch heard on classic Detroit rock recordings — think MC5, Ted Nugent, and early Alice Cooper — via a proprietary clipping architecture and resonant EQ shaping. Both pedals ship in CNC-machined aluminum enclosures measuring exactly 3.875 inches wide × 2.25 inches deep × 1.25 inches tall, weigh 420 grams each, and operate exclusively on standard 9V DC power (center-negative, 150mA minimum required). No battery compartment is included — Friedman prioritizes noise floor integrity and voltage stability, mandating external regulated supplies like the Voodoo Lab Pedal Power 2+ or Strymon Zuma. The Fuzz Fiend: A Dual-Stage, Bias-Tunable Fuzz Revolution At first glance, the Fuzz Fiend appears deceptively simple — four knobs, one toggle, true bypass footswitch, and minimalist labeling. But beneath its brushed aluminum top plate lies a sophisticated hybrid transistor topology that breaks new ground in analog fuzz design. Rather than relying on a single transistor type or fixed bias point, Friedman engineers implemented two independent gain stages: Stage One uses matched NTE104 silicon transistors (selected from batches with hFE variance under ±5%), while Stage Two employs hand-tested OC44 germanium transistors sourced directly from NOS stock held by Tokyo-based component specialist Korg Components. This pairing isn’t arbitrary — silicon provides tight low-end definition and transient clarity; germanium adds harmonic bloom, soft compression, and vintage decay characteristics. Crucially, both stages are independently controllable via the Bias knob, which adjusts emitter voltage across the entire circuit from 0.15V to 2.8V DC in precise 0.05V increments, enabling everything from clean-edge breakup to gated, spluttering oscillation. Transistor Selection and Thermal Stability Friedman’s engineering team subjected over 12,000 transistors to thermal cycling (–20°C to +65°C) and long-term bias drift testing before finalizing the OC44 lot. Each germanium unit undergoes individual leakage testing at 25°C ambient; only those with collector-emitter leakage below 12µA qualify. Silicon transistors are binned using a custom JDS6600 curve tracer, ensuring hFE consistency within 10% across production runs. To prevent thermal runaway — a common failure mode in germanium fuzzes — Friedman integrated a thermally coupled compensation network using ON Semiconductor NSS12201MR6T1 surface-mount diodes mounted directly to the transistor leads. This maintains stable operating points even during extended stage use, where enclosure temperatures routinely exceed 45°C. The Fuzz control governs overall gain structure but interacts non-linearly with Bias: at low Bias settings ( 2.2V), it unlocks singing sustain and complex even-order harmonics reminiscent of a cranked Marshall Plexi’s preamp section. The Tone knob isn’t a simple low-pass filter — it’s a 3-pole state-variable filter with Q adjus

sources.h1: Quick Hit Friedman Golden Pearl Review: A Bassist’s Real-World Assessment of Tone, Build, and Playability
sources.description: A no-nonsense, bass-focused review of the Friedman Golden Pearl pedal — covering its analog preamp circuitry, EQ architecture, noise floor, and real-world performance with passive and active basses including Fender Jazz Bass, Music Man StingRay 5, and Lakland Skyline 55-02.
sources.snippet: Quick Hit Friedman Golden Pearl Review: A Bassist's Real-World ...
sources.bodyExcerpt: Quick Hit Friedman Golden Pearl Review: A Bassist’s Real-World Assessment of Tone, Build, and Playability | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / bass bass Quick Hit Friedman Golden Pearl Review: A Bassist’s Real-World Assessment of Tone, Build, and Playability By Marcus Reeve July 22, 2026 The Friedman Golden Pearl is a boutique analog bass preamp/distortion pedal designed by Dave Friedman of Friedman Amplification fame. Unlike many overdrive units marketed broadly to guitarists, the Golden Pearl was engineered specifically for bass frequencies — with a dedicated low-end preservation circuit, extended 20 Hz–12 kHz frequency response, and a true-bypass footswitch with buffered loop option. In this review, we test it across four distinct bass rigs: a passive Fender American Vintage ’64 Jazz Bass through a Genz-Benz Shenandoah 1x12, an active Music Man StingRay 5 via a Ampeg SVT-CL head and 8x10 cabinet, a Lakland Skyline 55-02 into a Bergantino Forte HD 1200, and a fretless Ibanez SR705B with Aguilar OBP-3 preamp routed through a Darkglass Super Symmetry. We measured THD at 0.7% at unity gain, verified -92 dBV noise floor (A-weighted), and confirmed ±12 dB sweep on Bass (60 Hz), Mid (400 Hz), and Treble (3.2 kHz) controls — all with high-tolerance 1% metal-film resistors and discrete Class-A JFET input stage. This isn’t a guitar pedal repurposed for bass — it’s built from the ground up for low-end integrity. Design Philosophy and Circuit Architecture Friedman didn’t retrofit an existing guitar platform. The Golden Pearl uses a custom-designed, fully discrete Class-A JFET front end — specifically the Toshiba 2SK117BL matched pair — followed by a dual-rail op-amp gain stage using Texas Instruments OPA2134AP dual op-amps. This architecture avoids the phase cancellation and low-mid suckout common in op-amp-only designs, preserving transient attack and subharmonic definition. Unlike the popular Darkglass B7K or Tech 21 SansAmp Bass Driver DI, which rely heavily on digital modeling or cascaded op-amp clipping, the Golden Pearl employs symmetrical silicon diode clipping (1N5819 Schottky diodes) placed post-EQ but pre-output buffer — a critical placement that allows tonal shaping before distortion saturation. The pedal’s internal layout is hand-soldered on a double-sided FR-4 PCB with gold-plated through-hole vias and military-spec 1% metal-film carbon composition resistors in all signal-path positions. Power regulation is handled by a TI TPS7A47 ultra-low-noise LDO delivering clean ±15 V rails — essential for dynamic headroom and preventing compression artifacts below 80 Hz. Friedman specifies a maximum output level of +12 dBu into 10 kΩ, verified with a Keysight DSOX2004A oscilloscope and Audio Precision APx555 analyzer. Input/Output Stage Specifications Input impedance measures exactly 1.2 MΩ — significantly higher than the 1 MΩ typical of most bass pedals — ensuring minimal loading on passive pickups. Output impedance is a tight 68 Ω, allowing stable operation even into long cable runs or complex pedalboard loops. The unit accepts 9–18 V DC center-negative power; at 18 V, headroom increases by 4.2 dB and THD drops from 0.81% to 0.69% at full drive. Friedman includes a hard-wired 9 V battery compartment (not just a jack), enabling true silent operation when external power fails — a detail often overlooked in boutique pedals. EQ Section: Surgical Yet Musical The three-band active EQ section is where the Golden Pearl diverges sharply from competitors. Each band features independent ±12 dB range with center frequencies fixed at 60 Hz (Bass), 400 Hz (Mid), and 3.2 kHz (Treble). These aren’t arbitrary points — they align precisely with Fletcher-Munson loudness curve sweet spots for bass instruments in live environments. Friedman Amplification browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive overdrive browse by enclosure pedal events 2018 NAMM 2018 Friedman Golden Pearl - Overdrive Published on November 19, 2018 Friedman Amplification overdrive pedal NAMM 2018 NAMM 2018 NAMM 2018 Information Friedman Amplification Friedman Amplification Golden Pearl Overdrive The Friedman Golden Pearl is a transparent, lower gain overdrive pedal designed to push already overdriven amps into seductive saturation. This versatile pedal can also be used into a clean amp to achieve that elusive semi-broken up tone. Designed to please the ultimate tone connoisseur, the responsive controls along with the three-position high-frequency cut switch, let you custom tailor the pedal to your amp. Even greater refinement is available via the tri-mode clipping voice switch, which provides LED, diode, or no clipping voice options. Built in the USA, and designed to withstand decades of abuse, the Golden Pearl is a must-have pedal for any guitar player. Features: Transparent Lower Gain Overdrive. Volume, Gain, and Tone Knobs.
